slides.title: What's actually worth automating in your work
slides.text: Automating has a reward and it has a price, and almost nobody writes down both. The reward is calculated like this: minutes it takes, times how many times a month you do it, times twelve, divided by sixty. That gives you hours a year. It's the only unit you can use to compare tasks that have nothing to do with each other. The price is the hours it takes to build it, plus the hours it'll cost you to maintain every…
items: Elena runs an art supply store in Granada. She hates the quarterly VAT filing: four hours of agony, four times a year, sixteen hours annually. What she doesn't hate is answering "do you have it in stock?" on Instagram, because she doesn't…

slides.title: Practice: Write down for five days what you actually do
slides.text: For five straight working days, every time you finish something you'd already done before, write it down in one line. Write what it was and how many minutes, rounded to five. For example: "Answering a client on WhatsApp about the schedule — 5." "Entering an invoice into Excel — 10." "Looking up a material's price on the supplier's site — 5." Don't do it from memory at the end of the day. Memory is exactly where the…
items: In a note on your phone or a notebook open next to your keyboard. No spreadsheets.

Between thirty and eighty lines after five days, with many repeated and with different minutes between them. If you have fewer than twenty lines, you're not writing down the small stuff, and the small stuff is where the money is.

slides.title: Your first automatic flow in n8n
slides.text: n8n is pronounced 'en-eight-en' and it's a blank screen where you place boxes and connect them with arrows. Each box is called a node (node: one step in the process) and does exactly one thing. It can check the time, ask another program for a piece of data, decide whether a number is over 500, or send an alert. The whole drawing, with all its boxes, is called a flow (workflow: the complete process saved under a…
items: Rocío's flow is three boxes: 'at 8:00', 'ask what the dollar is worth' and 'write the sentence with the number'. Three boxes, one execution a day, thirty executions a month out of the 2,500 that come with the cheapest paid plan.

slides.title: Practice: Decide where your n8n is going to run before you touch anything
slides.text: There are only two reasonable answers today. (A) Their cloud: you go to n8n.io, create an account, and in two minutes you have n8n in front of you without installing anything. It's a 14-day trial, no card, and after that about €20-25 a month. (B) Your own computer: free forever, but you have to paste a line into the terminal. Plus, the flow only runs while the computer is on and n8n is open. Answer three questions…
items: In your head, with the browser open on n8n.io
One sentence written on paper or in a note: 'going with the cloud' or 'going with my computer'. Nothing more.

slides.title: Connecting two apps that don't talk to each other
slides.text: Gmail doesn't know your spreadsheet exists. And your form has no idea what Slack is. It's nobody's negligence: every application is a closed box, with its data inside. It only has one slit through which it can be talked to from outside. That slit is called an API: the window where one program serves another program, not a person with a mouse and keyboard. When you say "I want to connect Gmail to my spreadsheet,"…
items: Ruben had his two houses: Gmail with 43 emails a week and a Google sheet with six columns. What he did on Sundays — open the email, read, switch tabs, type — was exactly the third party's job. A human was doing it with a coffee next to…

slides.title: Practice: Write your connection as one three-part sentence
slides.text: Before opening anything, write the sentence: "When THIS happens, grab THESE FIELDS and do THIS OTHER THING." Be unbearably specific. "When an important email arrives" doesn't count: "when an email arrives whose subject contains New order and that comes from orders@myshop.com" does. If you can't write the sentence, it's not that you're missing technical skill. It's that you don't yet know what you want, and the AI…
items: On paper, or in ChatGPT's, Claude's, or Gemini's text box

A short spec sheet with six sections. What matters most is point 4. If the AI can't find a unique identifier, it'll tell you. That means you're going to get duplicates no matter what, and it needs solving before moving on.

slides.title: Putting AI inside the workflow
slides.text: Every node (each box in the workflow, each step) you've built so far always does the same thing. "Grab column C" grabs column C today, tomorrow, and ten thousand runs from now. "Send a message to Slack" sends it the same way every time. They're dumb, and that's their virtue: you can trust them without looking. The AI node doesn't work that way, and not because of some fixable flaw. It receives text you've never…
items: Rocio's workflow ran perfectly 400 times. Email 401 arrived in Catalan, the AI answered "Retorn," and the next node, which looked for the exact word "return," found nothing and left the workflow hanging. The email didn't get filed and…

slides.title: Practice: Write your workflow as one sentence and mark where a human decides
slides.text: Write your automation as a single sentence shaped like this: "When X happens, I do 1, 2, and 3, and it ends in Y." Real example: "When an email arrives at hello@inkandclay.com, I read it, decide what it's about, file it in its folder, and alert Slack if it's urgent." Now underline the part where today you read something and decide something. That part, and only that part, is where the AI node goes. If you underlined…
items: In a blank document or on paper

A list of 4 to 8 numbered steps, most marked mechanical and one or two as decisions. And a clear sentence telling you which is the candidate and what type it is. If it tells you your step is "classifying and also drafting," listen: that's…

slides.title: Keeping it from breaking: check, alert, and leave a trail
slides.text: When you do things by hand, failures announce themselves: you're right there, you see the red screen, and you fix it on the spot. Not an automation. It works while you sleep, while you eat, and while you're with your daughter at the park. When it breaks, nobody's watching. There are two clocks here: the clock of the breakdown (3:14 AM) and the clock of you finding out (nine days later). The one that matters is the…
items: If a message had reached Rocío's phone at 3:14 AM, she'd have seen it at 8:30 with her coffee. Filling in the phone by hand and hitting retry is four minutes. The difference between four minutes and a Saturday plus $400 isn't in the…

slides.title: Practice: List everything that could go wrong, before touching anything
slides.text: Describe your flow box by box, with the real names you gave each one. Don't ask it to fix anything yet: today you just want the list of possible breakdowns. Copy the prompt below and swap the flow description for your own. The more specific you are with sheet names, services, and field names, the more useful the list.
items: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in the chat with your automation

A table with twelve to fifteen rows, not five. At least three or four will surprise you. "Someone renames the sheet" and "the flow stops halfway" are almost never thought through. Save that table, it's the shopping list for the rest of the…

slides.title: What would prevent your project from being handed off?
slides.text: Use one case you actually observed. Name the evidence, the risk and the next check. There is no automatically correct option for this open question.
items: Missing evidence
Unreliable repeated event
Unknown permission
No recovery owner
